Netflix is not growing as expected. Users don’t open the app

Netflix's shares have slipped by about 29 per cent, affecting the company’s overall growth. Its advertising will also face a slump of about $300 million compared to its earlier projections.

Sagrika Kissu

26 October, 2026 05:38 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Netflix is losing out on its viewers. A Bloomberg report has noted that the once loyal army of Netflix users are not watching the streaming service as much as they did earlier.

“Customers aren’t opening the app on as many days a month as they did a couple of years ago, said the people who asked not to be identified because the data is confidential,” the Bloomberg report read.

The report added that the customers are also spending less time watching Netflix. While the total time on the app has increased, sources told Bloomberg that it’s because more customers were added. But individually, the users are watching less.

Show Full Article

“Netflix has increased its programming budget and is expanding into new categories, such as podcasts and live sports, to attract new customers and retain old ones,” said the report.

As per a firm named Apptopia, a firm that tracks mobile app use , the share of US subscribers who didn’t open the app rose by 16.6 per cent in the third quarter, compared to last year.

Netflix has not produced many hit TV shows and films this year. But its executives have identified several reasons behind this decline: new user interface to greater competition, worse programming to dearth of marketing outside the service.

And now, Netflix is worried. In 2022, the company started cracking down on password sharing. But the reason is not password sharing but users finding less value in the content on the platform.

“At first, executives assumed it would be short-term, because fewer people were using each account. But the trend has continued, raising the risk that people are using each account. But the trend has continued, raising the risk that people are finding less value in the service or spending more time with rivals,” the report said .

Also read: Does air pollution cause dementia? What new studies say on what it does to the brain

Not growing as fast as expected The decline in usage has been modest at 2 per cent. The shares have slipped by about 29 per cent, affecting the company’s overall growth. Netflix said its advertising will also face a slump of about $300 million dollars compared to its earlier projections.

Co-Chief Executive Officer Ted Sarandos said that viewership in the US is not particularly “growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.” But he added that the company is doing well outside the US.

Netflix was founded in August 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph to make movie rentals more accessible. Back then, it brought a major shift in the movie rental industry as people didn’t have to visit physical stores but could order DVDs online and get them delivered to their homes.

It was in 2007 when Netflix launched its streaming service “Watch Now.” It had a library of around a thousand movies and TV shows that users could watch online instantly.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)

Macron keeps lid on violence but public anger in France shows few signs of abating

The standoff leaves the govt in a quandary, with calls growing for more spending on services when it’s under pressure from a fast-growing debt burden & surging borrowing costs.

Alan Katz

26 October, 2026 05:25 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A fire breaks out at a demonstration in Paris, France, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

French President Emmanuel Macron bet that a massive police presence could avoid a repeat of the violence that stunned the country on Oct. 17. He won that wager, but isn’t any closer to resolving underlying anger that’s fueled mass protests in France and shows few signs of abating.

Hundreds of thousands took part in the demonstrations across consecutive weekends, with turnout remaining high despite worries about further violence, Macron’s warning against action unless organized by labor unions, and poor weather.

The standoff leaves the government in a quandary, with calls growing for more spending on services when it’s under pressure from a fast-growing debt burden and surging borrowing costs, and with presidential elections on the horizon.

Show Full Article

Student groups are continuing their call for further protests over what they say is the absence of concrete measures to address concerns about school conditions, needed funding, and the system for distributing university slots. Unions have called for a major day of strikes and protests on Nov. 5.

“We’re not giving up on anything,” Manon Moret, secretary general of student union UNEF, told reporters during the protest in Paris. “On the demands of young people, the €10 billion, and the issue of selectivity” in university placements.

But France doesn’t have the budget leeway to mount a dramatic financial response. While it dodged a downgrade by Moody’s Ratings on Friday, it’s struggling to reduce its yawning budget deficit ahead of the April election, and has seen borrowing costs jump as investors demand higher premiums to buy its debt.

A closely watched gauge of bond risk rose last week to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis. The spread between 10-year yields in France and Germany, the region’s safe asset, reached 178 basis points on Thursday, against 85 basis points at the start of September.

Protest Numbers There’s been no let-up on the demonstrators’ side so far. Some 410,000 people took part in the weekend marches across the country, according to the Interior Ministry, compared with its estimate of 550,000 for Oct. 17. The left-wing CGT union put its estimate much higher, at about 800,000 for each day.

On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he expected protests to continue. “From here till the elections, and in the very short term, the situation is extremely tense,” Nunez said on BFM TV, noting that some demonstrations have already been called for Oct. 31.

“Halloween evening is typically lively,” he said. “Of course we’ll deploy a very robust plan.”

The government has indicated it may shift its position, at least slightly, this week. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is scheduled to meet with student representatives on Monday after they’d been requesting a meeting for weeks. On Saturday, Finance Minister Roland Lescure floated the idea of advancing by a couple of months the annual increase in France’s minimum wage, which is indexed to inflation.

“Yes, we’re constrained financially,” Lescure said in an interview on Franceinfo radio. “But we’ve been creative.” He noted that the government had released strategic stocks of diesel and issued subsidies for high-mileage drivers to ease the pressure of high energy costs.

Read more: France Avoids Moody’s Downgrade in Reprieve After Week of Crisis

Macron’s government can at least consider how to convince protesters to stay home after the past weekend’s marches went ahead with far less violence than the week before, when authorities were caught flat-footed and demonstrations descended into chaos.

Rioters a week earlier attacked public buildings and broke into stores across the country, including in the capital, fought with police, and set fire to cars. Macron, the target of much of the anger, on Thursday acknowledged “planning failings and elements of surprise.”

As a result, the government deployed some 70,000 security officials on Saturday, including elite anti-terror forces. It also banned marches in several cities and forced demonstrators in Paris to take a route that confined them to the eastern edge of the city. A total of 1,435 people were arrested on Saturday, Nuñez said.

Next Saturday may be another test. At least one protest website has already called for another round of demonstrations on Oct. 31, while Union Syndicale Solidaires co-head Murielle Guilbert said she expected unions to call for new protests as well.

During the largely left-wing protests across France on Saturday, groups regularly shouted “Macron, resign!” The slogan also proved popular at the far-right National Rally’s congress in Orleans over the weekend. “Don’t worry,” party president Jordan Bardella said during a speech on Sunday. “He’ll be gone before long.”

Macron’s term ends in May, and term limits prevent him from running again in 2027.

A survey published in Le Parisien newspaper on Saturday showed that the National Rally’s candidate, Marine Le Pen, is firmly in the lead for that election, with far-left France Unbowed leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, in second place, ahead of various centrist contenders.

Speaking on Sunday, Le Pen basked in that advantage. “Everyone in France agrees with us; the battle is won over the assessment” of how France is doing, she said. “Our goal is to offer a real alternative, which is not a revolutionary act, but a natural cycle in democracy.”

Wider Protests Protests continued elsewhere in Europe during the weekend, too, over a range of issues including the cost of living, housing and education. About 100 people were arrested in central Barcelona, where protesters burned containers, vandalized shops, and threw stones at police.

Thousands marched in cities across Italy amid a heavy police presence, with scattered clashes reported. Albania’s capital of Tirana continued to be rocked by demonstrations against its prime minister. Tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets were used by police as protestors threw stones and set fires.
